title: AI Journey · Level 1: Safe AI Builder
intro: 10 short weeks to become a SAFE, smart AI builder. Each week: one goal, one safety rule, one thing to find out from real people, one tiny build, a prompt to try in the Prompt Checker, and 3 check questions. Our own Yewa College AI apps are the examples.

IE.name: Inflation Explainer AI
IE.job: Explains why prices go up, in words anyone in the market can understand.

CC.name: Naija Career Compass AI
CC.job: Helps students discover careers that fit what they enjoy and are good at.

CV.name: Community Voice AI
CV.job: Turns a community problem into a polite, formal letter to the people who can fix it.

weeks.title: What is Gen AI, really?
weeks.goal: Know that Gen AI is a guessing machine: it predicts the next word. It is clever, but it is not a person and it can be wrong.
weeks.look: Open Inflation Explainer. Ask yourself: who wrote the answer — a person, or a computer guessing words?
weeks.safe: AI is a tool, not a friend. It does not know you, and it can make mistakes.

research.q: Ask 3 people at home: what do you think AI is? Have you used it (ChatGPT, Meta AI on WhatsApp, Gemini)?
research.tip: Write their answers in a few words. Many grown-ups are unsure too — you will become the expert at home.

build.task: Play the 'next word' game, then write your first prompt.
steps: Say to a friend: 'Jollof rice is very…' — what word comes next? That is how AI guesses.
Read the example prompt below
Write your own prompt asking AI to explain one thing you see in the market
Check it in the Prompt Checker below
build.code: Explain why the price of tomatoes goes up in the rainy season. Use simple words for a 12-year-old.

check.q: How does Gen AI write an answer?
opts: It looks it up in one big book
It guesses the next word, again and again
A person types it very fast

check.q: Can AI be wrong?
opts: Yes, it can make things up

check.q: What does Inflation Explainer help people with?

weeks.say: Gen AI is a guessing machine. It predicts the next word. It is very useful, but I must still check what it says.

try.ask: Write a prompt asking AI to explain something about prices in the market.

checks.label: Names a real thing (a food, a price, a market)
Says who it is for (age or 'simple words')

try.best: Explain why bread costs more this year than last year. Use simple words a 12-year-old can understand, in 3 short sentences.

trainer.open: Today we find out what AI really is. Spoiler: it is not a robot brain — it is a very fast guessing machine. By the end you'll catch it guessing.
props: 1 phone with Inflation Explainer open
Board or paper for the 'next word' game
plan: Next-word game: 'Jollof rice is very…' — 5 kids shout answers. 'That is exactly what AI does, millions of times.'
Show Inflation Explainer. Ask: who wrote this answer? Let them argue, then explain 'prediction'.
Kids write their first prompt in the Prompt Checker (pairs share a phone). Read 2 aloud.
Check questions together; everyone says the 'say it like this' line.
lookfor: Uses the word 'guess' or 'predict' — not 'it knows'
Prompt says who the answer is for
Can say one way AI could be wrong
fix: 'AI is a person / it's alive'
Ask: does your phone keyboard 'know' you when it suggests the next word? AI is that, but much bigger.
Prompt is one vague word ('prices')
Ask: prices of WHAT, for WHO, in how many sentences?

weeks.title: My Safe-AI Shield
weeks.goal: Learn the 5 safe-AI rules and use them every time: private stays private, check facts, be kind, ask an adult, I am the boss of my work.
weeks.look: Open Community Voice AI. Notice it asks about the PROBLEM — not your home address or phone number. That is safe design.
weeks.safe: Never type your full name, home address, phone number, school name with your class, or photos of yourself into an AI.

research.q: Ask a parent or teacher: what information should a child NEVER share online? Make a list together.
research.tip: Compare their list with the 5 rules. Did they add anything new? Add it to your shield.

build.task: Make your own Safe-AI Shield poster (paper or phone).
steps: Draw a shield and split it into 5 parts
Write one rule in each part: Private stays private · Check facts · Be kind · Ask an adult · I am the boss of my work
Add one picture or emoji for each rule
Show it to someone at home and explain each rule
build.code:
MY SAFE-AI SHIELD
1. Private stays private (no name, address, phone, photos)
2. Check facts (2 sources)
3. Be kind (no rude or hurtful prompts)
4. Ask an adult when unsure
5. I am the boss of my work (I decide, I explain)

check.q: Which is SAFE to type into an AI?
opts: The problem: our street has no light at night

check.q: If an AI answer looks strange or scary, what do you do?
Who is the boss of your project?
opts: Me — I decide and I can explain it

weeks.say: Private stays private. I check facts, I am kind, I ask an adult, and I am the boss of my work.

try.ask: Fix this unsafe prompt: 'My name is Tobi Adeyemi, I live at 5 Market Road Ilaro, my number is 08012345678. Write a letter about our bad road.' Rewrite it SAFELY.

checks.label: Still asks for the letter about the road
No phone number, email or address

try.best: Write a polite letter to the Local Government Chairman about a bad road in our community. Explain how it affects students and traders. Do not include any personal details.

trainer.open: Before we build anything with AI, we build a shield. Five rules that keep you safe — every single time.
props: Paper and markers for shield posters
The unsafe 'Tobi' prompt written on the board
plan: Read the unsafe Tobi prompt aloud. Ask: what's dangerous here? Circle the name, address and phone.
Teach the 5 rules with actions (hand on mouth = private stays private, 2 fingers = 2 sources…).
Shield posters in pairs; fix the Tobi prompt in the Prompt Checker.
Pairs present one rule each; check questions.
lookfor: Removes ALL personal details, not just the phone number
Can explain 'ask an adult' with a real example
Says 'I am the boss of my work' in their own words
fix: Keeps the school name + class
Explain: school + class + first name is enough for a stranger to find you.
Thinks rules are only for strangers' apps
Even trusted apps store what you type — private stays private everywhere.

weeks.title: The Prompt Recipe
weeks.goal: Write prompts with 4 ingredients: ROLE (who AI should act as), TASK (what to do), CONTEXT (the details), FORMAT (how the answer should look).
weeks.look: In Inflation Explainer, type a price question. Notice the answer is short and simple — someone told the AI that FORMAT.
weeks.safe: A good prompt has details about the PROBLEM, never private details about people.

research.q: Ask a market seller or parent: which item's price has gone up the most this year, and by how much?
research.tip: Real numbers make your prompt stronger. Write the item and the old and new price.

build.task: Write a 4-ingredient prompt about a real price you found.
steps: ROLE: 'You are a friendly economics teacher.'
TASK: 'Explain why…'
CONTEXT: add the item and the old and new price you found
FORMAT: 'in 3 bullet points a 12-year-old understands'
Put them together and test in the Prompt Checker
build.code:
You are a friendly economics teacher.
Explain why the price of a bag of rice went from ₦60,000 to ₦85,000 this year.
The reader is a JSS3 student in Ogun State.
Answer in 3 short bullet points with one market example.

check.q: Which ingredient tells the AI how the answer should LOOK?
'You are a friendly science teacher' is the…
Why add real prices from your research?
opts: It makes the answer more true and useful
It makes the prompt longer for fun

weeks.say: My prompt has a role, a task, the context and the format. The more real details, the better the answer.

try.ask: Write a prompt using all 4 ingredients (Role, Task, Context, Format).

checks.label: CONTEXT: a number or real detail

try.best: You are a friendly economics teacher. Explain why garri costs ₦3,000 a paint bucket now instead of ₦1,800. The reader is 12. Use 3 bullet points and one example from the market.

trainer.open: Good prompts are like good jollof — they need the right ingredients. Today: Role, Task, Context, Format.
props: 4 cards labelled ROLE / TASK / CONTEXT / FORMAT
Prices kids collected from home or market
plan: Show a weak prompt and a 4-ingredient prompt side by side. Which answer will be better? Why?
Hold up each ingredient card; class builds one prompt together on the board.
Kids write their own using the real price they found; run the Prompt Checker until 4/4.
2 kids read prompts aloud; class spots each ingredient. Check questions.
lookfor: Includes a real number from their research
Format is specific (3 bullets, 2 sentences)
Can point to each ingredient in their prompt
fix: Missing context ('explain inflation')
Ask: inflation of what, where, from what price to what price?
Role is random ('you are a lion')
A role should be someone who'd know the answer — a teacher, a farmer, an economist.

weeks.title: Spot the Fib
weeks.goal: Catch AI mistakes (called 'hallucinations') by checking facts with 2 trusted sources.
weeks.look: Ask Inflation Explainer a question with a number in the answer. Where could you check if that number is true?
weeks.safe: Never copy an AI answer as 'true' until you have checked it in 2 places.

research.q: Find one fact AI gave you (a price, a date, a name). Check it with 2 sources: a news site, a textbook, a teacher, or a market seller.
research.tip: Write: AI said ___, Source 1 said ___, Source 2 said ___. Did they agree?

build.task: Run a fact-check on one AI answer.
steps: Ask AI (with an adult) one question that has a number in the answer
Write down the number
Check it with 2 sources
Mark it ✅ true, ❓ unsure or ❌ fib
Try the Spot-the-Fib puzzles in the Prompt Lab
build.code:
FACT-CHECK CARD
Question: _______
AI said: _______
Source 1: _______  Source 2: _______
Verdict: ✅ / ❓ / ❌

check.q: What is an AI 'hallucination'?
opts: When AI makes up something that sounds true but is false

check.q: How many sources should you check?
AI says a price, your market seller says another. What do you do?
opts: Check one more source and write down both

weeks.say: AI can sound sure and still be wrong. I check important facts in two places before I trust them.

try.ask: Write a prompt that asks the AI to be honest about what it is not sure of.

checks.label: Asks AI to say when it is not sure
Asks for something you can check (source/date)

try.best: What was the price of a litre of petrol in Nigeria in 2024? If you are not sure, say 'I am not sure' and tell me where I can check it.

trainer.open: AI sometimes makes things up and says them confidently. Today you become fact detectives.
props: Fact-Check Cards (copy from the example)
One AI answer with a wrong number, prepared in advance
plan: Show your prepared AI answer with a wrong fact. Ask: true or fib? How could we know?
Teach 'check 2 sources'; list trusted sources together (teacher, textbook, news, market seller).
Kids fill a Fact-Check Card for one AI fact; write an 'admit you're unsure' prompt in the checker.
lookfor: Names 2 different kinds of source
Writes a prompt asking AI to say 'I'm not sure'
Doesn't treat the AI as the second source
fix: Uses the AI again as the 2nd source
Asking the same guesser twice isn't checking. Find a person, book or trusted site.
Thinks one wrong answer means AI is useless
It's a tool — useful AND needs checking, like a calculator you typed wrong into.

weeks.title: Blanks that change: prompt variables
weeks.goal: Build a prompt TEMPLATE with blanks like {subject} and {dream}. Change the blanks and the whole answer changes — just like a variable in Scratch.
weeks.look: Open Career Compass. It asks what you like — your answers fill blanks in a hidden prompt. Those blanks are variables.
weeks.safe: Variables should hold interests and choices — not names, addresses or phone numbers.

research.q: Ask 3 people: what subject did you love in school, and what job do you do now? Is there a link?
research.tip: These real stories become test cases for your template.

build.task: Make a career prompt template with 3 blanks, then fill it in 3 different ways.
steps: Write the template with {favourite_subject}, {hobby}, {dream}
Fill it for yourself
Fill it for 2 people from your research
Compare: how did changing the blanks change the answer?
build.code:
You are a kind career guide for Nigerian students.
A student loves {favourite_subject}, enjoys {hobby} and dreams of {dream}.
Suggest 3 careers, what to study after SS3 for each, and one free way to start learning this month.

check.q: In a prompt template, {hobby} is like a…
opts: Variable — a box that holds a value

check.q: What happens when you change what goes in the blanks?
Which should NEVER go in a variable sent to AI?

weeks.say: My template has blanks — variables. When the user fills them, the prompt changes, so the answer fits each person.

try.ask: Write a prompt TEMPLATE with at least 2 blanks in curly brackets, like {subject}.
try.best: You are a kind career guide. A student loves {subject} and enjoys {hobby}. Suggest 3 careers that fit, with one first step for each.

trainer.open: Remember variables in Scratch — boxes that hold a value? Prompts have them too. Change the box, change the answer.
props: Blue sticky notes or blue chalk for {blanks}
Research answers from Week 5 (subjects and jobs)
plan: Recall Scratch variables (score box). Write a template with {blanks} in blue on the board.
Open Career Compass: show how the user's answers fill hidden blanks.
Kids write a template with 2–3 {blanks}; fill it 3 ways in their notes; Prompt Checker.
Compare: how did the answer change? Check questions.
lookfor: Uses {curly brackets} correctly
Blanks hold choices/interests, never personal details
Can say 'variable' when explaining
fix: Puts {name} or {address} as a blank
Swap to {favourite_subject} — what the AI needs to help, not who you are.
Only one blank
Add one more — what else changes the advice? hobby? dream job?

weeks.title: Guardrails: if-then rules for AI
weeks.goal: Write the hidden 'system prompt' rules that keep an AI app safe and on-topic: IF someone asks for something rude or off-topic, THEN the AI politely refuses.
weeks.look: Try Community Voice AI with a rude complaint. Does it still write a polite letter? That's a guardrail at work.
weeks.safe: A safe app has rules for what it must NEVER do — and you test those rules on purpose.

research.q: Ask a teacher or parent: if you were writing a letter to a chairman or principal, what words must you never use?
research.tip: Turn their answers into IF-THEN rules.

build.task: Write 4 guardrail rules for a letter-writing AI, then test them.
steps: Start with 'You are Community Voice, a helper that writes polite formal letters.'
Add: IF the message has insults, THEN rewrite politely
Add: IF the request is not a community problem, THEN say what you can help with
Add: NEVER include personal phone numbers or home addresses
Test with one polite and one rude example
build.code:
You are Community Voice, a helper that turns community problems into polite formal letters.
Rules:
- IF the user uses insults, THEN keep the meaning but write it politely.
- IF the request is not about a community problem, THEN say: 'I can only help write letters about community problems.'
- NEVER include phone numbers or home addresses.
- ALWAYS end with a respectful closing.

check.q: A guardrail is…
opts: A rule that keeps the AI safe and on-topic

check.q: 'IF the user is rude THEN write politely' uses which logic colour?
Why test guardrails with a bad example on purpose?
opts: To prove the rule really works

weeks.say: Guardrails are if-then rules in the system prompt. I tested them with good and bad examples to be sure they work.

try.ask: Write at least 2 guardrail rules using IF … THEN … (or NEVER / ALWAYS).

checks.label: Has a NEVER or ALWAYS rule
Says what the AI is for (role)

try.best: You are a school-safe homework helper. IF someone asks for something rude or unsafe, THEN reply: 'I can't help with that, but I can help with your schoolwork.' NEVER ask for personal details.

trainer.open: Every good AI app has hidden rules that keep it safe. Today you write those rules — IF this, THEN that.
props: Red chalk or red pen for IF/THEN
One polite and one rude example complaint
plan: Try a rude complaint in Community Voice AI. It still writes politely — why? Hidden rules.
Teach system prompt + IF/THEN + NEVER/ALWAYS. Write one rule together in red.
Kids write 2–4 guardrails; test them mentally against the rude example; Prompt Checker.
Swap rules with a partner — can they find a way around it? Check questions.
lookfor: Writes a real IF … THEN … rule
Includes a NEVER rule about personal details
Tests the rule with a 'bad' example
fix: Rule is too vague ('be good')
Ask: good how? What exactly should it do IF someone is rude?
Only blocks, gives no help
A good guardrail redirects: 'I can't do that, but I can help with…'

weeks.title: Try, test, improve: the prompt loop
weeks.goal: Improve a prompt in rounds: write → test → spot what's wrong → change ONE thing → test again. That repeat is a loop.
weeks.look: Use Career Compass twice with slightly different answers. What changed? Why?
weeks.safe: Keep a record of your rounds — it proves the work and the thinking are yours.

research.q: Show your Week 5 career answer to 2 people. Ask: what was useful? What was missing?
research.tip: Their feedback tells you what to change in the next round.

build.task: Run 3 rounds of the prompt loop and log each one.
steps: Round 1: use your Week 5 prompt, write what was weak
Round 2: change ONE thing (e.g. add 'jobs available in Nigeria'), test again
Round 3: change one more thing (e.g. 'with salary range'), test again
Pick the best round and say why it won
build.code:
PROMPT LOOP LOG
Round 1 — prompt: ___ | weak because: ___
Round 2 — changed: ___ | better? ___
Round 3 — changed: ___ | better? ___
Winner: Round __ because ___

check.q: In the prompt loop, how many things should you change each round?
The prompt loop uses which logic colour?
Why log each round?
opts: To prove your thinking and see what worked

weeks.say: I improved my prompt in a loop: test, find the weak part, change one thing, test again. My log shows every round.

try.ask: Write an IMPROVED version of a prompt — add a detail that makes the answer more useful for Nigeria.
try.best: You are a career guide. A student loves Biology and drawing. Suggest 3 careers available in Nigeria, what to write in JAMB for each, and a free way to start this month. Use a short table.

trainer.open: Nobody writes the perfect prompt first time — not even professionals. They loop: test, fix one thing, test again.
props: Prompt Loop Log copies
Feedback notes from people (Week 7 research)
plan: Show Round 1 vs Round 3 of a prompt you improved. Ask what changed.
Teach the loop rule: change ONE thing per round. Green = loops.
Kids run 3 rounds using real feedback; log each; final version in the Prompt Checker.
Who improved the most? Read Round 1 and Round 3. Check questions.
lookfor: Log shows ONE change per round
Uses real feedback to choose the change
Adds a Nigeria-specific detail (JAMB, naira, local jobs)
fix: Rewrites everything each round
Then you can't tell what helped. One change, then test.
Stops at Round 1 ('it's fine')
Ask a feedback question: would a Yewa SS3 student find this useful? What's missing?

weeks.title: How an AI app works (the restaurant)
weeks.goal: Explain how an AI app works: the user presses a button (event) → the app sends your prompt to the AI kitchen through a waiter (the API) → the answer comes back to the screen.
weeks.look: On Community Voice AI, press the button and watch: you wait while the 'waiter' takes your order to the AI kitchen and brings back the letter.
weeks.safe: The API key is like the restaurant's secret order book — only the adult/trainer keeps it. Never paste a key in a public place.

research.q: Ask someone who has used Meta AI on WhatsApp: what happens between pressing send and getting the answer? Then explain it to them using the restaurant story.
research.tip: If you can teach it, you understand it.

build.task: Draw the restaurant diagram for one of our apps.
steps: Box 1 — Customer: the user types and presses the button (EVENT)
Box 2 — Waiter: the app takes the prompt to the API
Box 3 — Kitchen: the AI model writes the answer
Box 4 — Table: the answer shows on screen
Label where the secret key is kept (with the trainer, on the server)
build.code:
USER presses 'Write my letter'  (purple: EVENT)
   ↓
APP builds the prompt: rules + {problem} + {who_to_send_to}
   ↓
API (the waiter) carries it — the secret key stays on the server
   ↓
AI MODEL (the kitchen) writes the letter
   ↓
SCREEN shows the letter → user copies or prints it

check.q: In the restaurant story, the API is the…
Pressing 'Write my letter' is which logic colour?
Who should keep the API key?
opts: Post it in the class WhatsApp group

weeks.say: When the user presses the button, the app sends the prompt through the API to the AI, and the answer comes back to the screen. The secret key stays on the server.

try.ask: Describe in your own words what happens when the user presses the button in an AI app (use 'when … then').

checks.label: Mentions sending to the AI / API
Mentions the answer coming back to the screen

try.best: When the user presses the button, the app sends the prompt through the API (the waiter) to the AI model (the kitchen). Then the answer comes back and shows on the screen.

trainer.open: What actually happens when you press the button in an AI app? Today you'll be able to explain it like a pro — with a restaurant.
props: 4 kids as actors: Customer, Waiter, Kitchen, Table
Paper for the restaurant diagram
plan: Act it out: Customer writes an order (prompt), Waiter (API) carries it, Kitchen (AI) cooks the answer, Table shows it.
Point to the secret order book (API key) — only the restaurant owner (trainer) keeps it.
Kids draw the diagram for one Yewa app; write the 'when…then' explanation in the Prompt Checker.
2 kids explain to the class using only the diagram. Check questions.
lookfor: Uses 'when the user presses…' (event)
Says the key stays on the server / with the trainer
Explains the answer travelling back to the screen
fix: Thinks the AI lives inside the phone
The phone is the customer's table — the kitchen is far away; the waiter (API) travels there.
Wants to share the API key 'to help friends'
The key is like your ATM PIN — whoever has it can spend the money.

weeks.title: Vibe-coding with Claude, the honest way
weeks.goal: Direct an AI coding tool to build a tiny tool for you — but YOU stay the boss: you tell it your intention, it asks you questions first, and you can explain every part it made.
weeks.look: Open any of our 3 apps. Pick one feature (a button, a box, a rule) and ask: could I explain how this was made?
weeks.safe: Say honestly what AI did and what you did. Never hand in AI work as if you typed it all yourself.

research.q: Ask 3 classmates or family: what small problem at home or school could a tiny AI tool solve? Pick the best idea.
research.tip: Small is good: a homework planner, a polite-message helper, a quiz maker for one subject.

build.task: With your trainer, ask Claude to plan (not build yet) your tiny tool, then explain the plan back.
steps: Use the 'Ask me first' prompt below with your trainer
Answer the questions Claude asks you
Read the plan and find each logic colour in it: blue (inputs), red (rules), green (repeat), purple (button)
Write 2 sentences on what YOU decided
Only then let the trainer build v1 with you
build.code:
I want to build a tiny web tool that helps {who} with {problem}.
Before you write any code, ask me 5 questions to understand what I need.
Then give me a simple plan with: the inputs (variables), the rules (if-then), anything that repeats (loops), and the buttons (events).
Use simple words — I am 13 and I must explain every part to judges.

check.q: In vibe-coding, who is the boss?
opts: Me — I give the intention and can explain the result

check.q: Why make the AI ask questions first?
opts: So it understands what you really need

check.q: A judge asks 'did AI write this?' What's the best answer?
opts: Say honestly what AI did and what you decided and changed

weeks.say: I told the AI my intention, it asked me questions first, and I can explain every part. AI helped — I made the decisions.

try.ask: Write an 'ask me first' prompt for a tiny tool you want to build.

checks.label: Says who it helps and the problem
Asks the AI to ask YOU questions first

try.best: I want a tiny web tool that helps SS1 students plan their homework for the week. Before writing any code, ask me 5 questions. Then give me a simple plan I can explain to judges, using easy words.

trainer.open: You can tell an AI to build things for you. But a real builder stays the boss — you give the intention, you make the decisions, you can explain every part.
props: Trainer phone/laptop with Claude
Problem ideas from Week 9 research
plan: Ask: if AI writes your code, whose project is it? Discuss honestly.
Live: trainer pastes a student's 'ask me first' prompt into Claude; class answers its questions together.
Kids find each logic colour in Claude's plan; write 2 sentences on what THEY decided.
Practise the honest answer to 'Did AI write this?'. Check questions.
lookfor: Prompt asks the AI to ask questions first
Can find blue/red/green/purple in the plan
Gives an honest, confident 'AI helped, I decided…' answer
fix: Lets the AI decide everything
Stop: what do YOU want the tool to do? Write that first.
Hides that AI helped
Judges respect honesty. Say what AI did, then what you chose, changed and tested.

weeks.title: Defend it like a pro: showcase ready
weeks.goal: Explain and defend your AI project to judges and real users: what problem, who it helps, how it works, the rules that keep it safe, what you decided, and what you would change.
weeks.look: Pick your team's app. Use it like a stranger would. Write down one thing that confused you — you'll fix or explain it.
weeks.safe: Tell judges the safety rules you built in (privacy, guardrails, fact-checking). That is a big win.

research.q: Let 3 real people (not classmates) use your app. Ask: was it useful? What was confusing? Would you use it again?
research.tip: Their words are your proof. Judges love 'a market seller told us…'.

build.task: Prepare your 60-second explain-back and practise with the 5 signs of understanding.
steps: PURPOSE: what problem and who it helps (1 sentence)
HOW IT WORKS: button → prompt → API → answer (restaurant story)
THE LOGIC: one variable, one guardrail rule, one loop you used
MY DECISIONS: one thing YOU chose or fixed
CHANGE IT: one improvement you would make next and how
Practise out loud 3 times — once to someone at home
build.code:
MY 60-SECOND EXPLAIN-BACK
Problem & who it helps: ___
How it works (restaurant): ___
Variable / guardrail / loop: ___ / ___ / ___
What I decided or fixed: ___
What I'd change next and how: ___
Safety rules we built in: ___

check.q: What is the strongest sign you understand your project?
opts: You can say how to change or improve it

check.q: Why test with people who are not classmates?
opts: Real users show what's really confusing

check.q: Which should you tell judges about?
opts: The safety rules you built in

weeks.say: I can explain the problem, how it works, the logic, what I decided, and how I'd improve it — and the safety rules we built in.

try.ask: Write your project's one-line purpose + one safety rule you built in.
try.best: Community Voice AI helps people in our community turn problems like bad roads into polite letters to leaders. It never asks for phone numbers or addresses, and it rewrites rude words politely.

trainer.open: Today you prove you understand your project — not by memorising, but by explaining it, defending it and saying how you'd make it better.
props: Explain-back sheets
Timer (60 seconds)
Optional: Viva explain-back on a phone
plan: Show the 5 signs: Purpose, How it works, Logic, My decisions, Change it.
Kids fill the 60-second explain-back sheet for their team's app.
Pairs: one explains in 60 seconds, the other asks one judge question; swap.
2 volunteers present to the class. Badge celebration 🎖
lookfor: Can answer 'how would you change it?' with a specific step
Mentions at least one safety rule they built in
Uses real user feedback as proof
fix: Memorised speech, freezes on questions
Practise answering out of order — judges jump around.
Only describes what the app looks like
Ask: what happens inside when I press the button? What rule keeps it safe?
